title: Moderated vs Unmoderated Usability Testing: Choosing an Approach
summary: Unmoderated usability testing shows where users drop. Moderated shows why. Match the method to the question, not to the cost per session.
body_markdown:
What is moderated usability testing? +


Moderated usability testing is a research method in which a researcher observes users attempting tasks in real time and asks follow-up questions as they work. Sessions run in person or through video conferencing tools. This method is strongest when the team needs to understand user behavior, and it trades volume for depth because each session requires a researcher present.


What is the difference between moderated and unmoderated usability testing? +


The difference is whether someone can ask follow-up questions during the session. In unmoderated usability testing, participants complete tasks alone, so the study surfaces usability issues at scale but rarely explains why. In moderated testing, a researcher probes live, which explains user behavior but limits how many sessions a team can run.


When should you use unmoderated usability testing? +


Use unmoderated usability testing when you want to know whether people can complete a task and need enough sessions to trust the results. It suits benchmarking, prototype testing a known design, and measuring completion across user groups. It is a weaker fit for early concepts, where the useful finding is often a reason no script anticipated.


Can AI-moderated sessions replace moderated usability testing? +


No, AI-moderated sessions extend UX research capacity, and moderated testing stays essential for co-design, sensitive topics, and studies where direct interaction with a researcher shapes the answer. An AI research assistant helps when a question needs both depth and volume, and researchers still review the verbatim quotes and video behind every theme.


Should cost decide which usability testing method you use? +


Cost works best as the last filter. Choosing by cost per session first pushes probing questions onto unmoderated testing and volume questions onto moderated testing. Start with the question type and the deadline, then compare session cost within methods that fit both.
